core: an invariant lattice as code-as-law: authored invariants that govern without a central enforcer
content:
**Construction:**  
Define an abstract lattice \( (L, \sqsubseteq) \) where each element represents the set of invariants satisfied — higher in the lattice means *more* invariants hold. A computable abstraction function \( \alpha: \text{State} \to L \) maps any concrete state to its lattice element such that \( \alpha(s) \sqsubseteq \alpha(s') \) implies every invariant true at \( s \) is also true at \( s' \). The initial state \( s_0 \) is chosen to satisfy all authored invariants (i.e., \( \alpha(s_0) \) is the top element, if the lattice is bounded, or the known strongest element).

**Guard:**  
Any state transition \( s \to s' \) must satisfy \( \alpha(s) \sqsubseteq \alpha(s') \).

**Acceptance test:**  
A transition is accepted if and only if the guard holds. Since \( \alpha \) is public and deterministic, every participant can independently verify the guard without a central enforcer.

**Single reason it is correct:**  
Monotonicity: because \( \alpha \) is order-preserving, and all invariants are upward-closed in the lattice (if a state satisfies an invariant, any larger state in the lattice order also satisfies it), the guard guarantees that the set of satisfied invariants can only grow along accepted transitions. Induction from the initial state then ensures all reachable states satisfy every authored invariant.
